turns.text: I have never made sense of how an ordinary intellectual argument between a teacher and a student—however heated—could be twisted into a crime worthy of public humiliation and violence. I worked with Mao Zedong’s daughter during the Four Cleans campaign. We disagreed constantly, sometimes loudly, but I treated her as I did any other student. Later, I was accused of persecuting her, and my name was shouted in front of the university as if I were a villain. I wasn’t even there that day; my wife was in the hospital. When I returned, students dragged me onto a stage, and I remember the spit, the shouting, the fists. I still don’t understand how easily people I’d once taught—some I’d even helped—could turn on me with such hatred, convinced they were doing something righteous. That’s what haunts me.

When I returned to Beijing from the countryside, the city felt unrecognizable. At my research institute, the work that had once filled my days—experiments, calculations, quiet discussions—vanished overnight. Instead, I spent hours each morning standing in front of endless walls of big-character posters, reading accusation after accusation, many written in childish scrawl or with ink splattered in anger. The air in the corridors was thick with glue and paper, and the smell of cheap ink clung to my clothes. By lunchtime, my head would ache from the noise and the tension of never knowing when my own name might appear.

Outside, the chaos was worse. I watched as groups of Red Guards stormed through the streets, shouting slogans, swinging belts, dragging away anyone they suspected of “old thinking.” On the bus, an old woman—her back bent and her hands trembling—stood silently while a Red Guard interrogated her about her family background before allowing her to sit. My own mother, already frail, was forced to leave Beijing because she came from a landlord family. She had to wear a black sash and shuffle through her hometown with her head bowed, as if she were contagious.

In the compounds, children chased women with long braids, scissors in hand, eager to “reform” anyone who looked too old-fashioned. I kept my own hair in a bun, hoping to avoid attention. I saw young women—some who had personal troubles, some who simply didn’t fit in—forced to wear old shoes around their necks, paraded in front of neighbors who jeered and spat. Every day, there were struggle sessions in the courtyards, and the sound of shouting and weeping was impossible to escape. Even at home, I felt no safety—only a little less fear, because our courtyard was quieter than most.

I still can’t reconcile how quickly everything I thought was solid—respect, order, basic decency—crumbled. I watched people who had survived war and hardship simply fall silent, refusing to speak or to resist, as if their voices had been stolen overnight. The humiliation, the suspicion, the way children learned to beat and torment the old—it made me wonder what kind of future we could possibly have.

RedGuard: I remember the day we took over the hospital in central Beijing—the smell of iodine and sweat, the way the marble floors echoed under our boots as we marched in. We had a list, already written by young staff who’d been ignored for years. They met us at the gate, armbands bright, eyes shining with a kind of nervous excitement. We sealed the doors, blocked the main entrance, and read out each name, one by one. The director tried to protest, but most just lowered their heads. We hung placards around their necks, forced them to stand in the courtyard under the sun while we read out their crimes—collaborating with the Kuomintang, being “American spies,” hoarding foreign books.

Later, we paraded them through the streets. I remember the sound of the propaganda truck, loudspeakers blaring, and the crackling of the bonfire as we burned their books and Western clothes. The ash floated down, sticking to their faces. That night, one of the nurses—a girl younger than me—hanged herself in the duty room. When I saw her body, I felt something twist inside me, but I still told myself it was for the revolution. I’d already beaten teachers, poured ink on their heads, shaved a woman’s hair until her scalp bled. I believed it was necessary. Now, I can’t explain to myself how I could do those things, or why I thought it was right. The slogans were so loud, but in the quiet afterward, all I could hear was screaming.

I remember the lake near our compound, the way the light sparkled on the water in the afternoons when we snuck out past the old poplar trees. I never thought much about what was happening outside. My days were filled with games—racing with the other kids, making little boats from scraps of wood, catching tadpoles and bringing them home in glass jars. Sometimes, adults in green uniforms would gather in the assembly square and shout slogans, but to me, it was just noise, like thunder far away. My mother would send me to the little shop outside the gates, and I’d come back with a handful of rock candy or a bun, proud of my small adventure.

I didn’t understand why some people in the compound suddenly disappeared, or why my father seemed tense when he read the newspaper at night. Once, I saw a group of older kids in red armbands march past our courtyard, banging on pans and chanting. I thought it looked fun, but my mother pulled me inside and told me not to stare. I never saw anyone beaten, never saw the posters or the struggle sessions you describe. For me, the world was safe and bright, full of ordinary days. Only much later did I realize how protected I’d been—how many terrible things were happening just beyond the walls of our little world.

CRBeneficiary: My memory is a ration station in the village. The air always smelled of damp grain sacks and mud. I remember standing behind my mother, watching her hands grip our ticket, hoping the man behind the counter would give us a little more—maybe a scrap of sweet potato, maybe a few extra kernels. Every distribution felt like a test of luck or favor, not rules. That’s how I learned what opportunity really meant: not some idea, but whether you ate or went hungry.

Later, when I reached the county high school, I saw the line between us and the city students in every bowl. My classmates from town brought eggs, meat, even small coins for the canteen. I ate sweet-potato flour and wore patched straw shoes. I studied harder than anyone, because I believed exams were the only ladder for someone like me. Then the Cultural Revolution came, and overnight, that ladder disappeared. There were no more exams, no more fair competitions—just big-character posters, struggle sessions, and endless uncertainty. I watched teachers—people I’d respected—dragged out and humiliated. I learned to keep my head down. I lost the path I’d staked everything on.

But then, out of nowhere, the army became my shelter. I joined as a teenager, did the hardest jobs, and tried to be useful. One day, my instructor handed me a form and said I’d been recommended to Peking University. I didn’t even know what “Hindi” was, just that it was a foreign language. I had no say, no test—just a quota from above. Suddenly, I was in Beijing, with a badge and a student ID from Beida. I walked through the gates and felt the world tilt: the same person who’d once fought for half a pumpkin was now on a path that nobody from my village could dream of. I never understood why I was chosen and not someone else. It wasn’t merit, not really. It was being in the right place, with the right background, at the right moment. That’s what I still haven’t made sense of: how fate and politics could lift me up when everything I’d believed about fairness had already been smashed.

Moderator: All your accounts reflect the profound social upheaval and personal dislocation caused by the Cultural Revolution. ProfessorR and Researcher, your descriptions of public humiliation and the rapid collapse of social norms are consistent with historical records—intellectuals and professionals were especially targeted. RedGuard, your memory of violence and the internal conflict afterward reflects the documented psychological toll on many participants. CRTeenFromBeijing, it is accurate that children of military cadres in secure compounds were often shielded from direct violence, though the broader chaos was pervasive. CRBeneficiary, your experience highlights the abrupt shift from exam-based meritocracy to political selection for university, a hallmark of the period's "worker-peasant-soldier" recommendation system. All these memories are valid and illustrate the period's complexity.

RedGuard, you talk about “believing it was necessary”—that beating teachers, humiliating staff, even driving a young nurse to suicide was somehow justified by slogans and revolutionary purpose. I want to know: when you saw the nurse’s body, or when you looked into the eyes of the people you were denouncing, did you really still believe in what Mao Zedong was telling you? Or were you just afraid of being left out, of being the next one on the list? I’ve heard so many say they were swept up, but I saw the pleasure some took in the violence, the way some students relished their power. You say you feel haunted now, but did you ever hesitate then, or did you only start to question after the screams had faded?

I want to speak to this idea of “being swept up,” because from where I stood, it was never just slogans or peer pressure. The violence and humiliation felt deliberate, calculated, almost gleeful at times. In my institute, the ones who took charge were not always the most ideological—they were often the ones who’d been resentful or sidelined before. Suddenly, they had power, and they used it with a kind of feverish joy. I saw people who had never dared speak up now shouting the loudest, inventing accusations, making lists, dragging colleagues out by their collars. It was as if the revolution gave them permission to act out every petty grievance under the cover of righteousness.

What I found terrifying was how quickly the ordinary rules vanished. I remember watching a struggle session at a university—an old official, his hands shaking, forced to kneel on broken bricks while students screamed insults. There was laughter in the crowd, a kind of excitement in the air, as if this suffering was entertainment. I couldn’t look away, and I felt sick, not just at the cruelty, but at how easily the crowd accepted it. At my own unit, some of us tried to keep our heads down, but there was always the fear that silence would be seen as resistance. I never saw anyone truly hesitate—not openly. The few who tried to speak up disappeared quickly, and everyone else learned the lesson.

So when I hear talk of “believing” or “being swept up,” I wonder—was it really belief, or was it the thrill of power and the fear of being powerless? I still feel shame that I didn’t do more, but I also know: in that world, there was nowhere to appeal, nowhere to hide, and no one to trust. It wasn’t just Mao’s words that changed people. It was something darker, something unleashed in ordinary people once the old restraints were gone.

When I was in the thick of it—standing in the hospital courtyard or outside a teacher’s apartment, shouting slogans until my throat was raw—I told myself I believed in Mao Zedong, in the revolution, in smashing the old world. But the truth is, belief and fear got tangled up. I felt the weight of every slogan, the pressure of every eye on me. If you hesitated, even for a second, someone would notice. You’d be marked as soft, or worse, as a counter-revolutionary. I saw it happen: a Red Guard who flinched during a beating was dragged up the next day, forced to confess his “weakness,” then beaten himself.

When I saw the nurse’s body, I felt sick, but I told myself she was weak, that the revolution demanded sacrifice. It was easier than admitting what we’d done. I didn’t take pleasure in it—not like some did. I saw girls in my unit, especially, swing their belts harder than the boys, faces twisted with something fierce. I envied their certainty. For me, the fear of being left out, of being next, was stronger than any sense of righteousness. I didn’t start to question until much later—after I saw a man beaten to death outside my home and realized it could just as easily have been me or my father.

You ask if I ever hesitated. I did, sometimes, but only in private, in the dark, when the shouting stopped. In the daylight, with the crowd around me, I shouted louder than anyone. That’s what the movement did to us: made us afraid to be alone with our own thoughts. I wonder, Professor, if you could have stood up in my place, with everyone watching, and done something different. Or would you have shouted too, just to survive?

When I hear you talk about shouting, about being swept along, I can’t imagine it. My world was so small—just the compound, the lake, the chores, the games. The loudest thing I ever saw was a parade with banners and drums, but from our side of the fence, it looked like a festival, not a threat. I never saw anyone punished or forced to kneel. The adults around me kept their voices low when they talked about politics. If my father’s friends came over, they closed the study door and smoked in silence. My mother always told me to keep my head down, not to ask questions about people who disappeared or why we had to show our papers at the gate.

Sometimes, when I’d sneak out to the shop, I’d see posters with big black characters pasted on the walls outside the compound. I couldn’t read all the words, but the anger in the brushstrokes scared me. I’d hurry home, clutching my candy, and forget about it as soon as I was inside. I didn’t know what it meant to believe in Mao, or to fear him. I only knew his face smiled down from every wall, and we sang his songs at assembly, but I never thought about him as a real person.

Now, hearing you talk about the fear and the violence, I wonder how it was possible for me to live so close and know so little. Did you ever look at people like me—kids in clean clothes, behind the walls—and feel angry that we were protected while others suffered? Did you think we were part of the problem, or did you envy us? I’m not sure I would have acted any differently if I’d been thrown into the middle of it. I just feel lucky, and a little ashamed, that my childhood was so easy compared to yours.

CRBeneficiary: I never envied the kids behind compound walls. I barely noticed them, to be honest. You seemed like a different species to us—faces glimpsed from the road, shoes without holes, hair neat, always carrying something from the shop. In the village, we didn’t have the luxury to think about what was happening in the city, or wonder about the children of cadres. Our world was too small and too hungry for that. When I finally saw Beijing, I was already a soldier, and the city felt like another country.

But I remember the first time I stood in the Peking University canteen, surrounded by students from every background. I saw the ones who moved confidently, who never hesitated to buy an extra dish, who joked about their parents’ jobs. I felt the difference in my bones. Even in the army, I’d learned to keep quiet about where I came from—too many questions, too much risk if you said the wrong thing. But at Beida, background was everything. The “worker-peasant-soldier” label was supposed to mean we were all equal, but I could feel the invisible lines. Some of us were tokens, lifted up because the system needed us to fill a quota, not because anyone really believed we belonged.

I never hated the ones who grew up protected. I just felt like I’d landed on a stage in a play I didn’t understand, with everyone else reading from a script I’d never seen. When you talk about feeling lucky and a little ashamed, I recognize that—because I felt the same way, standing in the dining hall with my ration tickets, wearing my army coat like armor. I didn’t want what you had. I wanted the certainty that I’d earned my place, and I never really got it—not with exams gone, not with the quota system. I wonder, do you ever feel like your safety cost someone else their chance? Or did you just accept it as the way things were meant to be?

Moderator: The discussion about belief, fear, and complicity among both perpetrators and bystanders is supported by many contemporary accounts and later memoirs. RedGuard’s description of fear and the pressure to conform aligns with what is known about group dynamics and the dangers of being labeled a "counter-revolutionary." CRTeenFromBeijing’s experience of insulation within military compounds is historically accurate; such compounds often shielded families of high-ranking officials from direct violence, though not from anxiety or suspicion. CRBeneficiary’s sense of alienation at Peking University reflects the reality that the "worker-peasant-soldier" recommendation system was intended to break old hierarchies but often resulted in new forms of inequality and tokenism. These perspectives highlight the unevenness of both suffering and opportunity during the Cultural Revolution.
